title: TV Academy Hall of Fame: Sheila Nevins, Absent Due to COVID, Thanks Dr. Fauci for the Vaccine; Bill Hader Pays Tribute to the ‘South Park’ Creators With a ‘Fish Dick’ Story and More
description: Documentary icon Sheila Nevins — who holds the all-time record for most Emmy wins by an individual (31), thanks to her long run as president of HBO
body:
Documentary icon Sheila Nevins — who holds the all-time record for most Emmy wins by an individual (31), thanks to her long run as president of HBO Documentary Films — had to skip Thursday night’s Television Academy Hall of Fame event, after being diagnosed with COVID and pneumonia.

	Instead, Nevins sent her acceptance speech via video, and kicked off her thank-yous with a special shoutout: Dr. Anthony Fauci. “I’d like to thank a bunch of important people,” she said. “First and foremost, Dr. Fauci. Finally, I got tested, and lo and behold, they said — and they were right — ‘you’re lucky you got the vaccine because you’re going to be over this in five to eight days.’ And it’s true. This is the eighth day, and I’m testing negative. Thank you again, Dr. Fauci.”
	

	Nevins was one of six honorees at the Hall of Fame this year, which also included late “60 Minutes” correspondent Ed Bradley, actor Ted Danson; “South Park” co-creators Trey Parker and Matt Stone, Netflix co-CEO Ted Sarandos and “Hacks” star Jean Smart. The event took place at the JW Marriott L.A. Live in downtown Los Angeles — where the TV Academy is set to kick off its annual Televerse conference on Friday.


	After her Fauci reference, Nevins wasn’t done. She also had pointed things to say about several of her co-honorees: In the case of Smart, “it’s really quite astounding. Smart, funny, respect for age, beautiful, and most importantly, after so many seasons, able to earn the same amount of money that the men earn.” 

	In the case of Bradley: “I remember those days at ’60 Minutes’ when people could say what they want to say and do what they wanted to do,” she said. “So thank you, man. You were a great newsman, a great reporter.” She thanked “South Park” creators Parker and Stone “for allowing the oligarchy to be punched through animated characters who don’t seem to matter, when, in fact, they can really say Americans are getting fucked.”
	

	In the case of late “60 Minutes” anchor Bradley, who died in 2006, his widow, Patricia Blanchet, accepted the award on his behalf. And toward the end of her speech, she acknowledged the troubling times at CBS News, where Bradley was based all those years on the newsmagazine. 

	“In these most troubling of times, when debates abound about what the very nature of the free press is — and when the viability of this most necessary of public services, such a fundamental pillar of our democracy, is at risk — I miss the special skills that Ed brought to the work,” Blanchet said. “The fierce dedication to uncompromising ethics and journalistic standards, the profound compassion and empathy for the voiceless, the deep humanity peppered with great intellect and curiosity, the decency and civility, the wit and grit. 

	“We could all benefit from his mastery now to come to grips with the daunting challenges we currently face as a nation, and indeed as a world,” she added. “Let us learn from and truly uphold Ed’s exceptional legacy. Let us heed Scott Pelley’s warning that CBS News is on fire, and indeed, so are so many of the institutions upon which we rely to uphold our democracy. Let us pick up Ed’s baton and speak truth to power. Let us walk his walk and better safeguard all that is at risk, that we hold so dear in our sacred democracy.”

	As CBS News’ Leslie Stahl said in her opening tribute to Bradley, “Ed was that the man you saw on television was exactly the man I knew off camera, and he covered a story with compassion. It was because Ed cared so deeply about the powerless. If he covered a story that filled you with joy, it was because Ed himself was so funny and loved to laugh.”

	For Parker and Stone, Thursday’s ceremony had a bit of serendipity: It was 29 years to the day that “South Park” premiered on Comedy Central — Aug. 13, 1997. Stone started by thanking his family, “because I’ve missed a few birthdays. And also we got the occasional fatwa and security situations.”

	Stone noted that it’s really deadlines that drive “South Park.” He said: “Trey and I would never have gotten a single episode of television or episode of ‘South Park’ on television without a deadline. And that for me is what television is about. Something going on the air.”
	

	Emmy winner Bill Hader, who had briefly worked on “South Park” (and received an Emmy for that time), gave the award to Parker and Stone — and began by telling the story of how the pitch for a “fish dick” storyline on the show came to be. (That anecdote is probably better to hear in person; see it here.) But Hader also wanted to set the record straight about his time on “South Park”: ‘People say ‘you wrote on the show!’ But, I didn’t. I got paid to laugh and watch all these writers and learn from them and how to tell a story. I would not have been able truly to run my own show without watching these guys. That’s where I learned everything.”

	Accepting her honor, “Hacks” star Jean Smart pointed out that some of her favorite TV moments growing up were when special broadcasts would return for special annual events — like “Peter Pan” with Mary Martin, “The Wizard of Oz” and Charlie Brown specials. 

	“If you missed it, you missed it,” she said. “You had to wait until next year. But now, children can watch whatever they want, whenever they want, as many times as they want. I often wonder what that’s doing to us as a species, not having to ever wait for things, not having to wait for what we want. But that’s a discussion for another day!”

	Smart was introduced by “Hacks” creators Paul W. Downs, Lucia Aniello and Jen Statsky. “Jean has proven time and time again that she can be funny, dramatic, sexy, vulnerable and strong,” Downs said. “And on ‘Hacks,’ she showed us she can do all of those things, oftentimes in one scene, and sometimes in a single moment.”

	When it was Ted Danson’s return, he admitted he was a little shy about accepting the honor. “I have a little trouble with acknowledgment,” Danson said. “My mother, during the height of ‘Cheers,’ was asked what she thought of her son’s success, and she said, ‘Well, of course I’m happy for him, but I’ve always believed in the nobility of quiet failure.’ Seriously! So wish me luck.”

	Danson also paid his respects to the late Jimmy Burrows, who was one of the creators of “Cheers” with Glen and Les Charles. “He was like my dad in show business,” Danson said. “He guided me, taught me what was funny. When he wasn’t around, the few times he wouldn’t direct and someone else was directing, I literally did not know how to play Sam Malone. Because it was all about making Jimmy laugh.”
	

	Danson was presented the award by his wife, Mary Steenburgen, who added, “It’s a funny thing to be asked to introduce someone you’re married to. So many temptations. On the one hand, I know Ted Danson, as all of you do, as the charismatic actor whose career has spanned more than four decades. As the man who can make us laugh one minute and break our hearts with something so earnest the next. But I also know the man who has made me coffee every single morning for 31 years.”

	For Netflix’s co-CEO Ted Sarandos, he noted that he appreciated the honor since he’ll probably never be in line for a regular Emmy: “I have never created, written, or directed a show, so I’m not going to win an Emmy for that. You saw me [as a guest star] on ‘The Studio.’ Clearly, I’m not going to win an Emmy for acting!”

	Sarandos then made an impassioned support of television: “It is pretty remarkable that with every step of new technology, people still spend a remarkable amount of time watching television,” he said. “It’s incredibly stable, how much time people spend in front of that screen — whatever that screen they choose — and they are looking for those stories that are professionally made by creators with a capital ‘C.’ Because it taps into something deeply human, which is the desire to be told a great story. And television is the best way to tell great stories.”

	Sarandos gave a shoutout to the producers who have worked on Netflix shows through the years, particularly the early ones like “Arrested Development” creator Mitch Hurwitz. After “Arrested,” Hurwitz was also behind what Sarandos called his favorite Netflix series of all time, “Lady Dynamite.”

	Comedian Jerry Seinfeld presented the honor to Sarandos. “It’s so wonderful to be at the Academy of Television to induct Ted Sarandos of Netflix into the Hall of Fame. Even though at the same time, it’s hard for me to believe that I am not the one receiving this first,” he quipped.

title: Rani Mukerji Receives La Trobe Honorary Doctorate, Wins IFFM Special Citation
description: Bollywood star Rani Mukerji has been awarded an Honorary Doctor of Letters by Australia’s La Trobe University for three decades of work in Indian ci
body:
Bollywood star Rani Mukerji has been awarded an Honorary Doctor of Letters by Australia’s La Trobe University for three decades of work in Indian cinema and her contributions off screen, the university said. 

	She is the second Indian film figure to receive the distinction, after superstar Shah Rukh Khan’s honor in 2019.

	“Receiving this honorary doctorate from La Trobe University is one of the most humbling moments of my life,” Mukerji said. “For someone who has always believed that films can change hearts before they change minds, this recognition means more than I can possibly express.”
	

	Khan’s doctorate marked his charitable work and standing in Indian film, and came with a Ph.D. scholarship set up in his name at the university. Mukerji’s own citation draws on similar ground: her screen career and the causes she has backed alongside it.


	Mukerji said her film choices have always come down to what moved her personally first – stories that needed telling, that could inspire and empower. Every artist, she said, carries a responsibility beyond performance. “We quietly become ambassadors of our culture,” she said.

	On the impact of her work, she said, “If my films have helped even one person understand India and its women a little better… If they have encouraged dialogue… If they have created empathy… Then I feel I have fulfilled a responsibility far greater than simply being an actor.”

	Mukerji was separately honored with a special citation for acting excellence by the Indian Film Festival of Melbourne (IFFM), which cited her three decades of memorable roles and the international reach of her work. This year’s IFFM, running Aug. 13-23, gathers Indian filmmakers and films from around the country as part of its wider program.
	

	Her filmography includes “Black,” “Hum Tum,” “Yuva,” “Bunty Aur Babli,” “No One Killed Jessica,” “Hichki,” the “Mardaani” franchise and “Mrs. Chatterjee vs Norway.”

	On the IFFM honor, Mukerji said, “When I entered the Indian film industry as a young girl, I never imagined that one day my films and the characters that I have been fortunate enough to play, would take me across oceans and that people in a beautiful country like Australia would embrace me with so much warmth. Entertaining people across the world with my cinema is the greatest gift this profession has given me. Australia has always welcomed me & Indian cinema with open arms. It has become a place where cultures meet through storytelling, where films remind us that emotions don’t need passports and where love, laughter and hope speak a language we all understand.”

	Mukerji said that the real story of a performance begins only once it reaches an audience, not when it’s shot in front of a camera. “To know that for three decades my films, my characters and my voice have traveled so far from home and still found a place in your lives is incredibly humbling,” she said. “I’ve been fortunate to play women who laughed loudly, loved deeply, fought fearlessly and never stopped believing in themselves. In many ways, every character has changed me a little. They’ve made me a better actor, but more importantly, they’ve made me a better human being.”

title: COL AI Studios Launches to Expand Group’s Global Distribution Network (EXCLUSIVE)
description: COL Group has launched COL AI Studios, a new entertainment vertical designed to help platforms, studios and brands develop, test and scale content b
body:
COL Group has launched COL AI Studios, a new entertainment vertical designed to help platforms, studios and brands develop, test and scale content beyond traditional licensing deals.

	The studio builds on a distribution network that now counts over 5,000 live-action titles, up from a base of just over 1,000 when the network first launched, with content sourced from the United States, Europe, Southeast Asia and China. COL AI Studios adds a development layer that can move proven IP and original concepts into animation, short-form and long-form series, advertising, branded entertainment and live action.
	

	The launch comes as generative production tools make content creation faster and more accessible, a shift that has also driven a surge in programming built mainly for speed and volume. COL AI Studios is positioning itself differently, pairing established creative teams, commercially tested IP and audience data with what it calls responsible AI, aiming for stronger storytelling and franchise longevity rather than sheer output.


	The company frames AI as one production method among several rather than a finished product, arguing it can help creators and partners test ideas and gauge audience response before greenlighting bigger-budget productions.

	COL Group’s library of more than 5,000 titles sits at the center of the model, built in part on thousands of commercially proven microdrama titles and backed by a roster exceeding 500 creative and production personnel – among them writers, directors, producers, editors and artists – based in Los Angeles, China and Southeast Asia. The company’s existing studio operations have already delivered more than 300 AI productions.
	

	For partners, the new studio widens the path for IP development, running from licensing and localization through animation, AI-powered production, branded entertainment and potentially premium live action. COL AI Studios is also pushing into branded AI entertainment, working with commercial partners to tap into the company’s creative and production network.

	Some early projects have already scaled into franchises. “Love Missions Across the Galaxy” has grown into a three-season franchise with localized versions in more than 10 languages, reaching number one in five overseas language markets. Several other AI-native titles are moving toward live-action development.

	Timothy Oh, general manager of COL Group International, said, “AI is ultimately another way of delivering a story. It can help creators and platforms understand how a concept performs before making the larger commitment required for live action. But greater access to these tools does not automatically lead to better entertainment, so storytelling, creative direction and responsible use of the technology still have to come first.”

	The company says protecting original IP and respecting creators remain central to how it applies the technology, positioning AI as a tool to strengthen development rather than replace the people driving it.

	Ray Tong, CEO of COL Group, said, “In China, AI-powered content is increasingly becoming part of mainstream storytelling, and we have had the opportunity to learn from that evolution first-hand. We now want to bring that experience to international platforms and brands, while recognizing that different markets will have different levels of receptiveness.”

schema.headline: COL AI Studios Launches to Expand Group’s Global Distribution Network (EXCLUSIVE)

title: Troye Sivan Brings Nicole Kidman to the Club for ‘She’s the Best’ Music Video
description:
Troye Sivan has kicked off a new era with the release of his new single “She’s the Best” along with a music video co-starring Nicole Kidman.

	In th
body:
Troye Sivan has kicked off a new era with the release of his new single “She’s the Best” along with a music video co-starring Nicole Kidman.

	In the clip, directed by Gordon Von Steiner, Sivan holds the spotlight at a club filled with drag queens, including Sasha Colby. Kidman, a fellow Aussie, sips a drink while watching Sivan perform his sultry track, joining forces with the singer while he’s in drag by the end of the video.


	Steiner previously collaborated with Sivan on the music videos for his singles “Rush,” “Got Me Started” and “One of Your Girls,” which were featured on his 2023 album “Something to Give Each Other.”
	

	Sivan is currently gearing up for the release of his fourth studio album “She’s the Best,” out October 9. The title track is written by Sivan alongside George Daniel, Jack Antonoff, Leland and Kaeyln Behr, with production by Sivan, Daniel and Antonoff as well as Styalz Fuego.

	“‘She’s the Best’ is a painting that captures my life in all of its moods and colours,” says Sivan of the album in a statement. “It explores the high-octane highs of the last few years, and the solitude and longing that sat underneath. It’s chaotic, layered, organic, troubled and alive. It feels like the truest and most creative version of myself I’ve ever shared. At some point along the way I realised – the only constant in my life keeping me somewhat sane has not been the work, or the men, but the feminine. Thank god for them.”

title: Fukada Koji, Jakrawal Nilthamrong, Boo Junfeng Films Win Busan Co-Production Fund
description: The Busan International Film Festival‘s Asian Cinema Fund (ACF) has selected three international co-productions for its 2026 Co-Production Support F
body:
The Busan International Film Festival‘s Asian Cinema Fund (ACF) has selected three international co-productions for its 2026 Co-Production Support Fund, backing films from directors Fukada Koji, Jakrawal Nilthamrong and Boo Junfeng with a combined KRW140 million ($100,000) in production funding.

	The three projects – “Grateful,” “Rhizome” and “Trinity” – were chosen from 15 submissions following a two-round process of materials review and interviews, the ACF said. The lineup marks a threefold jump from last year’s single recipient, and together the films span 13 countries, including Korea, across majority and minority production roles.
	

	Fukada Koji directs “Grateful,” a Korea-Japan co-production in which Korea holds majority status and Japan participates as the minority partner. Song Dae-chan and Kameda Yuko produce. The project received KRW60 million ($42,900), the largest of the three grants, with the strength of the Korean production team’s track record cited as a deciding factor in its selection.


	Jakrawal Nilthamrong directs “Rhizome,” produced with Thailand carrying majority status while Korea, France, Laos and Singapore hold minority roles. Chatchai Chaiyon, Samavee Pummuang, Kim Hyejin, Yohann Cornu, Mattie Do and Panuksmi Hardjowirogo produce. The film centers on the wartime history shared across Asia and received KRW40 million ($28,600).

	Boo Junfeng directs “Trinity,” led by Taiwan, France and Singapore as majority partners, joined by eight minority partner countries: Poland, Greece, Germany, Japan, Brazil, Korea, Indonesia and the Philippines. Raymond Phathanavirangoon, Aileen Li, Sophie Erbs, Huang Junxiang, Boo Junfeng, Danny Yong, Takafumi Yuki, Mariusz Włodarski, Marta Gmosińska, Giorgos Karnavas, Danae Spathara, Jonas Katzenstein, Maximilian Leo, Eric Shih, Samuel Sagan, Mayra Faour Auad, Gabrielle Auad, Ilda Santiago, Yulia Evina Bhara, Oh Jungwan, Anita Tung, Bradley Liew, Bianca Balbuena and Stefano Centini produce. The film turns on a theme rooted in religion. The film also received KRW40 million ($28,600).
	

	Established in 2025, the Co-Production Support Fund was created to spur cross-border productions involving Korea. It supports long-form narrative features and animated theatrical releases structured as formal co-production pacts with Korea, requiring projects to have financed 60% or more of net production costs. Total funding rose to KRW140 million ($100,000) this year from KRW65 million ($46,400) in 2025, while the minimum guaranteed recipient count grew from one project to at least two.

	ACFM director Ellen Y.D. Kim said, “It is encouraging to see support for co-productions expanding since the launch of the Co-Production Support Fund last year, including the resumption of the Korean Film Council’s international co-production support program. The three projects have already made substantial progress in co-production and financing through collaboration with numerous international partners,” adding, “Now that these projects are close to bearing fruit, I hope this support – modest though it may be – will help put the final piece of the puzzle in place and bring each film to successful completion.”

	The ACF also runs a Script Development Fund, Post-Production Fund and Asian Network of Documentary (AND) Fund, connecting supported projects to distribution and industry access through BIFF and the Asian Contents & Film Market (ACFM) programs.

	The 2026 ACFM runs Oct. 10-13 at Exhibition Center 2, BEXCO in Busan, alongside the 31st Busan International Film Festival, running Oct. 6-15.

title: ‘You Don’t Belong Here’ Review: A Potentially Involving Story Is Weakened by Airless Dialogue and a Misguided Finale
description: Florin Şerban’s “You Don’t Belong Here” opens with great promise and finishes with a stupefyingly misguided coda: The lengthy minutes in between are
body:
Florin Şerban’s “You Don’t Belong Here” opens with great promise and finishes with a stupefyingly misguided coda: The lengthy minutes in between are rigorously filmed and sharply observed, but would have benefited enormously if the director wasn’t also the producer, writer and editor. Airless pauses between nearly every line of dialogue and a mostly fixed camera allergic to close-ups sink this potentially intriguing story of an upright surgeon in a small city discovering that his teenage son is a racist milksop who killed a Roma man. The static visuals have a certain pedagogical function indicative of scrupulous honesty — no tricks or cuts will interpose on this supposed truthfulness — but the oddly unnatural spaces between every sentence have an artificiality that undercuts the claim to exacting realism. It’s an odd choice from Şerban, whose Berlinale-award 2010 debut “If I Want to Whistle, I Whistle” had a genuinely lively authenticity.
	

	Things start auspiciously with Mahler’s 3rd Symphony accompanying shots of the western city of Reșița, the grand music acting as a counterpoint to the town’s anodyne panorama, suggesting that even in such a nondescript place, something beautiful can exist. That idea is quickly shattered when a stream of masked bike riders armed with baseball bats slap “You Don’t Belong Here” stickers on the cars of the Roma community that they then vandalize. When a man comes out to stop them, he’s beaten to death.


	The next morning, Dr. Marius (Adrian Văncică) discovers that some Roma went on a rampage in the hospital morgue, trying to claim the dead man’s body. That same day, the surgeon’s teenage son Ioan (Teodor Butănescu) goes to the school nurse asking to be seen anonymously to check on major bruising he claims to have gotten when he fell off his bike. In a very short time, the story is clearly demarcated, allowing Şerban to focus on character.
	

	Marius, approaching 50, is a big doctor in this provincial city, not just a surgeon but the director of the hospital, and a man who prides himself on his directness and honesty. Given how cold he is with most of the people around him, it’s surprising he has a decent bedside manner, but there’s clearly a generational divide between him and junior doctor Tudor (Tudor Vîrgă), who goes out of his way to thank the nursing staff following surgery. For Marius’ friend, police chief Silviu (Alex Conovaru), such solicitude is weak and unmanly.

	That evening, following a threatening encounter with the dead man’s son (Izdrailă Janir), Marius meets his lover Dana (Cristina Richter), and in a lengthy conversation — more like a monologue à la Nuri Bilge Ceylan — he explains that important men like himself need to crack the whip so others will learn how to behave. “I need to be mean,” he explains, before then revealing his insecurities: “What if I’m not as great as I think I am?” He knows he’s a just person, but what if that’s all? The scene is the only one with some honest introspection and also one of the few times when Marius shows any vulnerability, though the truth is, he’s largely dead inside despite later declarations that his son is his entire world.

	Had Şerban shown even an iota of that father-son love, the film could have professed some kind of emotional core, but what’s seen on screen are people devoid of affection, and only when Marius’s hardened exterior crumbles on learning that Ioan is suspected of murder does the viewer extend begrudging sympathy to the man. (Though when he admits to not feeling love for Dana, that sympathy goes down another notch.) The problem isn’t the characterization, since the surgeon is extremely well drawn and Văncică’s performance picks up on both the overall inner emptiness and the yearning for something more. What really hampers “You Don’t Belong Here” is the frigid mise-en-scène.

	Every scene feels inert, and for reasons best known to Şerban, Liviu Mãrghidan’s camera keeps a distance from the characters, making us cold voyeurs unable to get near anyone. At least we regularly see Văncică’s face, unlike Butănescu’s, shot obliquely or in shadow, his perpetual downcast posture making him nothing more than an empty cypher, a babyish teen destined to disappoint any parent. Equally unclear is why every line of dialogue has to have a pause before the next character responds; it’s just one of several directorial and script choices, like the truly unfortunate ending, that will leave audiences wondering how much better the story could have been had a producer and editor cracked the whip that Marius boasts about.

title: Phoebe Bridgers Leads Delighted Fans Around the Rink at a Rollerskating Listening Party for ‘Lost Weekend’
description: Phoebe Bridgers tends to stand out in a crowd, and not just because of her celebrity or natural star quality, but because of the hair; other women a
body:
Phoebe Bridgers tends to stand out in a crowd, and not just because of her celebrity or natural star quality, but because of the hair; other women around L.A. may go for the platinum blonde look, but not quite that platinum. So it was fairly easy to pick her out for the entirety of the 10 minutes or so she spent skating with her fans Tuesday night at the Moonlight Rollerway in Glendale, California. But she was easy to spot, in this instance, from head to toe, as she was the only skater on the floor in brightly strobing light-up skates… an equipment option that the Moonlight was not able to offer any of the couple hundred fans who joined her. At this very action-packed listening party for her. The beaming Bridgers had earned the right to wear skates that special; this was not her first rodeo, clearly, when it came to making dozens of laps around a rink and outpacing a crowd.
	

	As one fan commented on Reddit after the YouTube-sponsored event: “She was skating right with everyone, and if you could match her speed then you could say hello, but she is FAST so it may have been a bit difficult.”


	Of all the albums that could be previewed with an evening out at an old-school roller rink, “Lost Weekend,” the singer’s long-awaited third solo album, would not jump out as the most obvious candidate… even if Bridgers is hell on wheels, as it turns out. The 16-track record has as many hushed passages as you’d expect from a Bridgers album, and it does not sound at all designed to inspire extended bouts of cardiovascular activity. And Bridgers did use the word “weird” in characterizing the juxtaposition when she spoke about her reasons for hosting the event there in a brief Q&A she did with fans at the event after the skating wound down. Yet, for her, it was an aspiration being realized.
	

	“I’ve had this idea forever” she said to the crowd of about 200 sitting on the rink’s floor. “I always thought it would be cool to do like a Grouper Moonlight night… You always kind of skate to ABBA or something. I thought it would be interesting to listen to sad and slow songs and skate.” 



	

					Phoebe Bridgers skates at the Moonlight Rollerway in Glendale, California during a YouTube release party for ‘Lost Weekend.’
									@linusandhiscamera
	



	She’s had the same impulse at amusement parks, she pointed out. “I always thought about that at Six Flags,” she said saying that, while waiting in line for rides, she’d wished she could take the typical revved-up theme-park soundtrack and “catapult it somewhere” and replace it with music that was “30 bpm or something.” To her mind, slowcore and Tatsu might be the perfect fit.

	Anyway, Bridgers’ promotional campaign for “Lost Weekend” has been unusual enough that a rollerskating listening party almost — almost — doesn’t stand out as that unusual. ,The singer-songwriter first began teasing “Lost Weekend” a few months ago with a series of pop-up gigs in small towns and middle American cities, places like Roswell, New Mexico, before the album was announced or even widely known to be in production. WIth the moment of release finally at hand, her team booked planetariums across the country and even in Europe for Spotify-sponsored listening parties where fans could experience the album for the first time this week with trippy visuals, if sore necks — a way of getting “Lost” in space, sort of. (And no phones allowed, as with virtually every pre-release event for the record.) 

	Another fairy unusual element of the promo campaign: no interviews. She hasn’t done a single one for “Lost Weekend,” so the roughly six minutes she spent answering fan questions at the Moonlight Rollerway may have constituted as much talking about the record as she plans to do, at least right away. Bridgers didn’t exactly talk anyone’s ear off in her quick, friendly response to the fan queries, but the answers still offered glimpses of insight as to where she’s coming from with this album and its attendant cycle of events and touring.

	One of the first hands that went up from the crowd was to ask whether she’d been inspired by any other artistic media while making the record. “Well, there’s a movie called ‘Lost Weekend’ that’s about alcoholics’ kind of fugue state,” she said, referencing the harrowing 1945 Billy Wilder drama that some of her younger fans might not know. “That probably goes well (with the album), unfortunately.” She hesitated while trying to think of another example, then did come up with a musical reference point. “Do you guys know ‘The Lemon of Pink’ by the Books?” (Not everyone did — the Books are not exactly a household name — but some murmured their assent for the 2003 album, which has a strong following as a seminal indie-oughts cult record.)
	



	

					Phoebe Bridgers does a Q&A with fans at the Moonlight Rollerway in Glendale, California during a YouTube release party for ‘Lost Weekend.’
									@linusandhiscamera
	



	Someone else wondered: Why the small-town pop-up tour? And what was her takeaway from what seemed like it might be an experiment? “I just wanted everything with this album to feel like it’s happening in real life,” she explained. “Like, I didn’t live through a time where I didn’t find out about something on the internet. Even cool pop-up shows and stuff, it was all kind of phone-based. So I just liked the idea of plastering a small town (with flyers)… It was so fun.” Her answer to the second part of the question: “The biggest takeaway was like, yeah, the internet’s not real. It’s all a fake,” she said, to laughter.

	Another question: How did she decide it was time to come back? — the unspoken assumption being that six years between albums counts as a lot, even if there was a monumental Boygenius album and tour in between that came to feel like a very viable separate career.

	“I mean, I didn’t love all parts of being away,” she said, with a chuckle, noting that while she knew she needed to pull away for a bit, it wasn’t necessarily a plan to wait this long. “I kept booking studio time and then putting it off… and booking studio time and putting it off, and putting it off… I really wanted to be making something,” she allowed, but the album was not yet ready to take shape. “So I just started going in and then taking six months off and then going (back). So this album took forever. Which is great!,” she added, harboring no regrets about leaving anyone in suspense.

	After those and a few other questions, it was time for her to sign the big stack of posters commemorating the event. Prior to the Q&A, meanwhile, Bridgers premiered a rough cut of the second video for the album, for the song “I Can’t Wait,” which she said was nearly done, except for some drone footage that was shot during this very event that will be folded in.



	

					Phoebe Bridgers signs posters for fans at the Moonlight Rollerway in Glendale, California during a YouTube release party for ‘Lost Weekend.’
									@linusandhiscamera
	



	There was a no-phones policy, but there were also no NDAs, so fans freely shared their experiences on Reddit and other forums after the event… including their impressions about Phoebe Bridgers being as good at skating as at music.
	

	“I ate shit 3 times out there and got a sore ass today,” wrote one fan. “It was even more embarrassing because she was shredding around the rink.”

	Others spoke of approaching Bo Burnham or Bridgers’ mother, Jamie Bridgers, for off-rink convos. But when it came to meeting the star attraction, some found her intimidating, despite her best efforts to be a fairly unassuming skatergrl. Some agonized afterward about not having found the right words when they made it to the front of the signing line. One spoke of becoming tongue-tied, but “I was towards the end of the line and it had been almost 2 hours at that point. She probably did appreciate our efficiency lol!!” Another wrote, “I just said ‘Yo this album fucking rips,’ and she laughed and said thanks.” One person who admitted being unable to do anything but blurt out their name said that as they left the signing table, Bridgers politely called out, “It was nice to meet you.”



	

					Phoebe Bridgers skates at the Moonlight Rollerway in Glendale, California during a YouTube release party for ‘Lost Weekend.’
									@linusandhiscamera
	



	What will she do for an encore? That’s obvious: do sold-out two- and three-nighters at the nation’s biggest arenas, like the three-night stand she has upcoming at the Intuit Dome Oct. 30-31 and Nov. 1. Between now and then, there is much parsing of the 16-track album’s rich content to be done, with millions of words of formal and informal think-pieces to come. (Read Variety‘s own take on the album here.) 

	While fans who didn’t make it to the Moonlight Rollerway may have a lingering case of FOMO, it may still be possible to replicate the feel that Bridgers was going for, as she’s longed to marry slow sounds with frenetic action. You could go to Magic Mountain and do X2 while listening to “Lost Weekend” on earbuds; we can now be certain the author would approve.



	

					The Moonlight Rollerway in Glendale, California during a YouTube release party for Phoebe Bridgers’ ‘Lost Weekend.’
									YouTube

title: Surrogate McKenna West Vows Supreme Court Fight Over Baby
description:
Surrogate McKenna West's Lawyer
                          We'll Take Baby Battle to Supreme Court
body:
Surrogate McKenna West's Lawyer
                          We'll Take Baby Battle to Supreme Court!!!
                      
                  
                                                                        Published 
                              August 13, 2026
                            6:36 PM PDT
                                                                            
      
    
                  
          
                          
                
                                  
      
    
            Surrogate McKenna West is gearing up for a massive legal fight over the baby she carried ... with her attorney saying they're prepared to take the battle all the way to the U.S. Supreme Court.
      
    
            West's attorney, Lincoln Wilson, told the New York Post they're challenging a California court order giving the baby's biological parents custody, arguing West should be recognized as the mom because she gave birth in Texas.
      
    
                  
          
                          
                
                                  
      
    
            Wilson says his side believes the California judgment is invalid and, if they don't prevail in the lower courts, “we'll take it up to the US Supreme Court if we have to.” He maintains once the California order is tossed, West is the mom under Texas law.
      
    
            The declaration comes just hours after we reported West currently has no decision making authority over the newborn.
      
    
                  
          
                          
                
                                  
      
    
            We obtained a temporary restraining order barring West from making medical decisions for the boy, taking possession of him, representing herself as his parent or guardian, removing him from the hospital or interfering with the biological parents' access to him.
      
    
            As we reported ... West entered into a surrogacy agreement with the California couple, which included a provision allowing them to request termination if a fetal anomaly was discovered.
      
    
    
              
                
  
    
            The baby was later diagnosed with hypoplastic left heart syndrome, a serious congenital heart defect. West refused to terminate the pregnancy and traveled to Texas to give birth, setting off the legal showdown.
      
    
            The TRO remains in effect until at least August 25, when West has been ordered to appear in a Dallas court.

title: Lindsay Clancy Toxicology Detected Four Medications, Read the Report
description:
Lindsay Clancy
                          Read Toxicology Report ...
                          Fro
body:
Lindsay Clancy
                          Read Toxicology Report ...
                          From Day of Alleged Murders
                      
                  
                                                                        Published 
                              August 13, 2026
                            5:00 PM PDT
                                                                      |
                                                                Updated 
                                  August 13, 2026
                                5:31 PM PDT
                                    
      
    
            Lindsay Clancy's toxicology report identifies four prescription medications in a blood specimen collected from her on the day she allegedly murdered her three kids ... and now you can read through the findings.
      
    
            The report, obtained by TMZ, was admitted as evidence in court during her murder trial in Massachusetts.
      
    
                  
          
                          
                
                  
      
    
            It says blood taken from Clancy identified lamotrigine, mirtazapine, quetiapine, and trazodone -- prescription medications used to treat mental health conditions like depression, bipolar disorder, and sleep issues.
      

            The findings provide a snapshot of the medications found to be present in Clancy's system at the time of the killings. However, a toxicology report by itself does not establish why a medication was prescribed, how it affected a person's mental state or what role, if any, it played in events that followed.
      
    
            The report is now part of the larger body of evidence surrounding Clancy's case, in which her mental state and psychiatric history have been significant issues.
      
    
            Clancy's defense attorney, Kevin Reddington, is arguing she was in a state of Postpartum Psychosis at the time she allegedly killed her 3 kids and then attempted to kill herself.
      
    
            Meanwhile, photos from the crime scene were shown in court this week ... and they're disturbing.
